newsitem.title: UK: UK regional manufacturing export optimism down - CBI.
newsitem.headline: UK regional manufacturing export optimism down - CBI.

text.p: Optimism about export prospects over the coming year has fallen sharply amongst UK manufacturers in 10 out of 11 regions over the four months to July, the Confederation of British Industry said on Tuesday.
"The high value of sterling is undoubtedly the primary cause of weaker exports, averaging 2.91 deutschemarks compared with 2.75 in the April survey," the CBI said in a press release.
The survey showed that manufacturing orders remained flat or fell in five of the 11 UK regions over the four months to July.

The survey by CBI and Business strategies, the regional economic consultancy, showed that manufacturing orders fell or remained flat in Wales, the West Midlands, the South West, North West, and Yorkshire and Humberside, with Wales reporting the sharpest decline. Firms in the North and Northern Ireland reported the strongest growth.

The survey said a decline in export orders was largely to blame for weak total orders. All regions were affected, with the sharpest falls experienced by manufacturers in East Anglia, Wales, the South West, Yorkshire and Humberside, West Midlands, and the North West.
"The regional picture in manufacturing reflects the situation in the national economy, where there is a clear divide between strengthening domestic demand and weaker exports.
"In three regions, Wales, the West Midlands and the South West, domestic demand is not strong enough to compensate for the decline exports," the CBI said.

In seven out of 11 regions, an increasing number of firms report that price competition is likely to constrain their ability to win export orders over the next four months. Firms in the East Midlands, East Anglia and Yorkshire and Humberside were most affected with almost 90 percent of those surveyed reporting that price competitions would limit export orders over the coming months.

Manufacturing output increased in six regions over the four months to July, with East Anglia, Northern Ireland and Scotland reporting the highest growth - a reflection of the increase in total new orders in these regions. Three regions, Yorkshire and Humberside, the North West and West Midlands, reported a modest growth in output despite having seen no increase in total new orders.

Firms in nine out of 11 regions expect output to increase over the next four months, with seven of the nine predicting higher output growth than in April. East Anglia and the South West have the highest growth expectations whilst manufacturers in Wales and the East Midlands are predicting lower output.

Manufacturers in seven out of 11 regions indicated that they would invest more in plant and machinery over the next twelve months compared with the last twelve months. Firms in Scotland and the South East expressed the strongest intentions.
There was a small increase in the number of firms working below capacity at the national level due to the impact of the gradual slowdown in output growth identified in the last three surveys.
